title: HTML Character Entities
summary: HTML entities let you show reserved characters and special symbols in text.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: `<` displays the less-than sign `<`. Without the reference, the browser may treat a following word as the start of an HTML tag. It is like quoting a symbol so it is read aloud instead of treated as an instruction. This is especially useful when teaching HTML or showing code examples. For example, write `<button>` when showing an opening tag as visible text.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: `>` displays the greater-than sign `>`. Together, `<` and `>` can show angle brackets around a tag name as visible text. They work like quotation marks around a symbol. When displaying user-provided content, use safe text APIs and established escaping instead of building HTML strings by hand. For example, use UTF-8 for ordinary language characters rather than memorizing many numeric references.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: `&` displays an ampersand `&`. The ampersand also begins many character references, so writing it directly in some attribute values can make the text ambiguous. It is like a punctuation mark that also starts a special instruction. Escape it when needed, especially in URLs and hand-written markup. For example, escape an ampersand in a URL when it separates query parameters in HTML markup.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: Modern HTML documents usually use UTF-8, which can represent a wide range of characters directly. You do not need to memorize a reference for every accented letter or symbol. It is like using a keyboard that supports the character rather than looking up a code. Ensure the document declares the correct encoding. For example, insert user-provided strings as text instead of building an HTML fragment.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Use character references when a literal character could be mistaken for markup or when a named reference improves clarity. They do not replace safe handling of untrusted input. Think of them as spelling instructions for the browser. For user text, insert it as text content so the browser does not interpret it as HTML. For example, check how a code example appears in the browser after escaping its punctuation.

foundations.overview: HTML has special characters that also have meaning in markup. Character references, often called entities, let you display those characters as text. For example, `<` displays `<` instead of starting a tag. Think of the reference as an escape label that tells the browser, “show this symbol.” Use UTF-8 for ordinary text and references where a character could be read as markup.
foundations.whyItMatters: Character references clarify symbols that would otherwise be parsed as markup. Knowing when they help—and when safe text insertion is better—prevents display and security mistakes.
foundations.browserPerspective: During tokenization the parser scans for &; when it sees one it tries to resolve a character reference and substitutes the corresponding Unicode character into the text node. If the reference is malformed it may be left as literal text. The declared charset determines how the remaining raw bytes become characters.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Entities appear everywhere: copyright lines in footers (©), code documentation showing tags (<div>), pricing with non-breaking units (10 €), trademark symbols, em dashes, and arrows. Templating engines auto-escape user input into entities to prevent XSS.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct escaping prevents broken pages and XSS vulnerabilities that can leak user data or damage trust. Proper encoding ensures international content displays correctly, broadening reach to global audiences.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding entities is essential for writing documentation, building templates, and sanitizing user input. Auto-escaping in frameworks (React, Vue, server templates) is built on the same concept.
foundations.performanceImpact: Entities are resolved cheaply during parsing and have negligible performance cost. Declaring UTF-8 lets you type most characters directly, keeping markup shorter and more readable than entity-heavy text.
commonUseCases: Escaping < > & to display literal code or math
Non-breaking spaces to keep numbers and units together
Numeric references for emoji, arrows, and non-Latin characters

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must use entities for accented and special characters like é or ©.
commonMisconceptions.reality: With <meta charset="UTF-8"> you can type most characters directly. Entities are required only for the reserved characters (& < and, in attributes, the delimiting quote); for everything else they're optional.

It's a non-breaking, non-collapsing space — it never wraps to a new line and multiple of them don't collapse into one. Using it for general layout spacing is an anti-pattern; CSS margins/padding are correct.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Character references sanitize every unsafe HTML string.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Escaping a few characters is not a substitute for safe text APIs or a vetted sanitizer.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every non-ASCII character requires an entity.
commonMisconceptions.reality: UTF-8 supports a wide range of characters directly when the document encoding is correct.

visualExplorer.title: How the parser resolves an entity
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through how <, &, and © are scanned and replaced with the literal characters they represent.

config.intro: When the HTML parser reads text, it watches for the ampersand that begins a character reference and turns it into a single character.

steps.name: Scan for &
steps.detail: As the tokenizer reads a text node it looks for an ampersand, which signals the start of a possible character reference.

steps.name: Read until ;
steps.detail: It collects the characters up to the semicolon — a name like 'copy' (named) or a number like '169' / 'xA9' (numeric).

steps.name: Resolve the reference
steps.detail: Named references map to a predefined Unicode code point; numeric references use the code point directly in decimal or hex.

steps.name: Substitute the character
steps.detail: © becomes ©, < becomes the literal < (NOT a tag start), and the result is stored in the text node.

steps.name: Render literally
steps.detail: Because < arrived as an entity, the browser shows the symbol instead of trying to open an element — that's why escaping prevents broken markup.

interactiveExamples.title: Reserved characters vs. their entities
interactiveExamples.explanation: The first line tries to type < and & literally; notice how it can confuse the parser. The second line escapes them, so the symbols render exactly as intended.

files.index.html:
Without escaping (ambiguous)

The expression a < b && c > d may not show correctly.

With entities (correct)

The expression a < b && c > d shows literally.

Symbols you can't easily type

© 2024 — Acme™ · 50 %

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Two paragraphs comparing unescaped vs. escaped text, plus a line showing ©, an em dash, ™, a middot, and a non-breaking space.

interactiveExamples.title: Named vs. numeric entities
interactiveExamples.explanation: Every entity has a numeric equivalent. Here © is written four ways — they all render the same character — and a snowman and arrow show numeric-only symbols.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A list showing © produced four different ways, and a line with a snowman, a right arrow, and the pi symbol.

codeLab.title: Display a literal code snippet
codeLab.instructions: This page is supposed to show the text `link` literally inside the block, but the angle brackets are being parsed as a real link. Escape the reserved characters so the markup is shown as text.

files.index.html:
To make a link, write:

link
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
code { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 6px; border-radius: 6px; }

codeLab.expectedOutput: The code block displays the literal text link instead of rendering a link.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
code { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 6px; border-radius: 6px; }

hints: Inside the code you can also escape the quotes with " for clarity, though they aren't strictly required here.
